title: How I Built a Telegram Bot That Downloads YouTube Music & Videos (Up to 2 GB) And How yt-dlp Actually Bypasses YouTube's Protection
author: CHANDAN
summary: Live Bot: @songsuperzxbot Source Code: github.com/chandan0000001/music-video_telegrambot HD Demo: Watch on Streamable I built a Telegram bot that downloads music and videos from YouTube and I want to walk you through exactly how it works, including the part that most tutorials skip: how yt-dlp actually gets past YouTube's stream protection. I built a Telegram bot that downloads music and videos from YouTube — and I want to walk you through exactly how it works, including the part that most tutorials skip: how yt-dlp actually gets past YouTube's stream protection. You can try the live bot here: @songsuperzxbot on Telegram Full source code: github.com/chandan0000001/music-video_telegrambot The Problem With Every Other Telegram Music Bot Most Telegram music bots you find online have the same three problems: They stop working after a few days because YouTube changes something They hit Telegram's 50 MB limit and either fail silently or send a compressed garbage file They run on a single thread, so if three people use it at once, everyone waits I wanted to fix all three. Here's how. How YouTube Stream Extraction Actually Works (The "Bypass" Explained) This is the part nobody explains properly. When you open a YouTube video in your browser, the actual MP4/audio stream isn't directly accessible at a clean URL. YouTube obfuscates it in two ways: 1. Signature Cipher YouTube wraps the stream URL inside a JavaScript function that scrambles the signature parameter. The raw URL looks something like this: ( https://rr3---sn-xxx.googlevideo.com/videoplayback?...&sig=SCRAMBLED_SIG ) The actual playable URL only works when you un-scramble that signature. YouTube's own player does this in the browser using a JavaScript function it downloads fresh every session. The function changes regularly to break scrapers. yt-dlp's solution: It downloads YouTube's player JS, extracts the current cipher function, reverse-engineers the transformation steps (they're always a combination of reverse, swap, and splice operations), and applies them to reconstruct the real signature. This is why yt-dlp updates so frequently — YouTube rotates this function. 2. n-parameter Throttling Even with a valid signature, YouTube adds an n parameter to the URL that limits download speed to about 50 KB/s if not decrypted. yt-dlp decrypts it using the same JS extraction approach, unlocking full speed. In my bot , I run yt-dlp with 8 parallel fragment streams to max out the download speed: ydl_opts = { ' concurrent_fragment_downloads ' : 8 , ' cookiefile ' : ' cookies.txt ' , # handles age-restricted content ' quiet ' : True , } The cookies.txt handles age-restricted videos. You export your browser cookies with the Get cookies.txt extension and drop the file in the bot's folder. What Happens After Download: The FFmpeg Pipeline Once yt-dlp pulls the raw stream, FFmpeg takes over. For audio: # Extract audio and convert to MP3 at chosen bitrate ffmpeg - i input . webm - vn - ab 320 k - ar 44100 output . mp3 For video, I use Intel VAAPI hardware acceleration when available, which runs about 10x faster than CPU encoding: # Hardware-accelerated H.264 encode ffmpeg - vaapi_device / dev / dri / renderD128 \ - i input . webm \ - vf ' format=nv12,hwupload ' \ - c : v h264_vaapi \ - c : a aac output . mp4 On machines without VAAPI (Windows, Termux, most VPS), it falls back to software encoding automatically. The 50 MB Telegram Limit — How I Send Up to 2 GB Standard Telegram bots can only send files under 50 MB. Most bots just compress the video into a potato-quality file. Mine doesn't. The routing logic works like this: Under 48 MB → Send directly via standard Bot API. Instant. Over 48 MB, MTProto configured → Use native MTProto client (Telethon) which supports up to 2 GB natively with your API ID and hash from my.telegram.org Over 48 MB, no MTProto → Split the file into 44 MB chunks using lossless stream copy (zero re-encoding, zero quality loss, runs at disk speed) The lossless chunking command looks like this: ffmpeg - i input . mp4 - c copy - f segment \ - segment_size 46137344 chunk_ % 03 d . mp4 No quality loss. No waiting for re-encode. Just pure stream splitting. Database: Why SQLite Was the Right Choice I went with SQLite in WAL mode instead of PostgreSQL. For a single bot, this was the right call: WAL mode means readers and writers don't block each other — critical when multiple users are downloading simultaneously Zero ops overhead — no separate database server to manage Atomic crash recovery built in Every connection opens with: conn . execute ( " PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL " ) conn . execute ( " PRAGMA foreign_keys=ON " ) The schema tracks every user, every search, every download, and aggregated stats in real time. Security: Blocking SSRF Attacks When users send URLs, a naive bot would just forward them to yt-dlp. That's dangerous — someone could send http://192.168.1.1/admin and probe your internal network. My validator rejects anything that isn't a real YouTube URL: YOUTUBE_REGEX = re . compile ( r ' ^https?://(www\.)?(youtube\.com/watch\?v=|youtu\.be/| ' r ' youtube\.com/shorts/)[A-Za-z0-9_\-]{11} ' ) def validate_url ( url ): # Block private IP ranges first if re . match ( r ' https?://(localhost|127\.|10\.|192\.168\.|169\.254\.) ' , url ): return False return bool ( YOUTUBE_REGEX . match ( url )) Filenames are also sanitized before hitting the filesystem to prevent path traversal: safe_name = re . sub ( r ' [^\w\-_\. ] ' , ' _ ' , raw_name )[: 200 ] Running 24/7 on Android (Yes, Really) One of the coolest deployment options is Termux on Android. No root required: pkg install python ffmpeg -y python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate pip install -r requirements.txt termux-wake-lock python bot.py The termux-wake-lock command prevents Android from killing the process when the screen turns off. I ran it for a week on an old Redmi phone and it handled hundreds of downloads without a single crash. The Test Suite: 30 Tests in 4 Seconds Everything is tested — URL validation, filename sanitization, FFmpeg processing, rate limiting, cancellation, and the database: pytest tests/ -v # 30 passed in 4.01s The cancellation test is my favourite — it verifies that hitting the Cancel button actually kills both the yt-dlp subprocess AND the FFmpeg process immediately, then confirms the temp directory is cleaned up. No zombie processes. Try It Yourself Live bot: https://t.me/songsuperzxbot on Telegram Source code + full setup guide: github.com/chandan0000001/music-video_telegrambot If you have questions about the yt-dlp cipher extraction, the MTProto upload integration, or running it on Termux, ask in the comments. Happy to go deeper on any part.

title: I Built a 170-Year Caribbean Hurricane Observatory, Alone, in Python
author: Dim's Build
summary: TL;DR CaribScope is an open-source climate risk observatory for the Caribbean: 170 years of Atlantic hurricane tracks (NOAA HURDAT2, 1851–2022), live USGS earthquake data, sea surface temperature trends, and a Random Forest model that predicts a storm's Saffir-Simpson category. It's a 16-page Streamlit app, built solo, running on a single VPS. It's also, by my own admission, more finished as a product than as a project anyone has heard of — which is the part of this post that isn't a victory lap. The gap During hurricane season, the National Hurricane Center and NOAA publish everything you'd want: forecasts, historical tracks, advisories. All of it in English, built for a US audience. French-speaking Caribbean media, creators, and residents get none of that tailored to them — no French-language dashboard, no historical context localized to Guadeloupe, Martinique, or Haiti, nothing that says "here's what a storm like this one has historically done in your part of the Caribbean." That gap is what CaribScope tries to close. 170 years is a lot of inconsistent data HURDAT2 is NOAA's official Atlantic hurricane database, going back to 1851. The format is a flat text file, not a clean CSV: header lines mixed with position/wind/pressure records, missing pressure values before the satellite era (pre-1979 mostly relies on ship and land station reports), and storm identifiers that changed convention more than once across 170 years. There's no off-the-shelf pandas reader for this — parsing it means writing a state machine that tracks whether the current line is a storm header or a data row, and being honest with yourself about which columns are trustworthy back to 1851 and which only become reliable once aircraft reconnaissance and satellites show up mid-20th century. The payoff for going back that far isn't just the feat itself. It's context: when a Category 3 approaches, "the last comparable storm hit this island in 1928" is a more useful sentence than "here's a live radar loop," especially for an audience that already has access to the radar loop. What's actually in it Trajectories & stats — every HURDAT2 storm, filterable by island, category, decade Seismic map — live USGS feed, magnitude ≥ 2.5, Caribbean plate boundary Climate trends — temperature and sea surface temperature (SST) over time ML prediction — a Random Forest classifier (scikit-learn) trained on the HURDAT2 history, predicting Saffir-Simpson category from a storm's current attributes Hurricane of the Day — a daily-format page pulling from the historical archive, built to be the shareable/embeddable unit for media and social 16 Streamlit pages in total, each independently a small app. Streamlit's multi-page routing (a pages/ folder, each file a page) made that structure nearly free — the cost shows up later, in navigation and information architecture, not in the initial build. The stack Python 3.10+, Streamlit for the app itself, Plotly for every chart and map, pandas / numpy / pyarrow for the data layer, scikit-learn for the Random Forest, pytest for tests. Shipped as a Docker image ( python:3.12-slim ) behind Coolify on a personal VPS, with GitHub Actions running CI and Renovate keeping dependencies current — the same self-hosted infrastructure I already run Listmonk on, so adding one more container was marginal cost, not a new operational surface. The Random Forest, and its actual limits The prediction model takes a storm's current attributes and outputs a predicted Saffir-Simpson category, trained on the historical HURDAT2 record. I want to be specific about what that is and isn't: it's a classifier trained on a few thousand historical storm-observations, not a physics-based forecast model, and it will never compete with NOAA's own operational forecasts, which fold in atmospheric modeling this project has no access to. What it's useful for is pattern-matching against history — showing, from data, what tends to happen next to storms that looked like this one before. That's a narrower and more honest claim than "hurricane prediction," and it's the one I'm making. What doesn't work yet The product is ahead of its distribution, not the other way around, and I'd rather say that upfront than have someone else point it out. Sixteen pages, a working ML pipeline, live earthquake and climate data — and until recently, no analytics installed, no email capture, no one outside a small circle who knew it existed. Building the thing was the easy part. The next phase is entirely about getting it in front of the people it's actually for: French-speaking Caribbean media and creators during the exact six months a year they'd want it. Try it Live app: caribscope.fwicss.fr Source: github.com/FWICSS/caribscope It's open source. If you've got a dataset that would sharpen the risk picture for a specific island, or you've dealt with HURDAT2's pre-satellite-era gaps before and have opinions, I'd like to hear them.

title: A Privacy Budget for Email Test Data
author: Lewis
summary: A Privacy Budget for Email Test Data Email is often treated as harmless test plumbing. A CI job creates an inbox, a verification message arrives, a test reads the link, and the inbox is forgotten. In practice, those messages can contain names, account identifiers, reset tokens, invite URLs, and enough product detail to reconstruct a user journey. The useful question is not “Which disposable inbox should we use?” It is “How much email data does this test actually need, for how long, and who can see it?” That is a privacy budget: a small, explicit limit on exposure that still lets engineers diagnose failures. This framing is helpful for teams building web applications because it joins Privacy and Security with maintainability. The cheapest data to protect is the data we never retain. Why email test data deserves a budget Test email has a strange lifecycle. It starts as synthetic data, becomes a delivery artifact, then turns into a log attachment or a screenshot. Each copy has a different audience and retention period. A mailbox that is safe for a local smoke test may be a poor fit for a shared staging environment. I use four questions to set the budget: Content: Does the test need the whole message, or only a token and delivery timestamp? Lifetime: Is the message needed for seconds, one CI run, or a week of investigation? Reach: Which people and systems can read the inbox, traces, logs, or artifacts? Reuse: Can one inbox accidentally reveal another test's message? If the answer is vague, the data budget is already too large. The implementation get messy when a test stores a complete email simply because the assertion was easier to write that way. Define the budget before choosing a tool For a normal verification test, a reasonable default might be: one generated address per test or isolated worker; one expected message, with a bounded wait; a retention period no longer than the CI run; logs containing message ID, subject hash, and timing, but not the body; a failure artifact containing a redacted excerpt only when the test fails. This is not a universal policy. An OAuth flow may need a link target, while a rendering test needs HTML and CSS. The point is to name the minimum capability instead of granting an entire persistent mailbox. Teams also need a vocabulary for search terms and operator mistakes. A developer may type tempail while looking for a temporary inbox, but that typo should never become a reason to broaden a production allowlist or retain more data. Small details like this prevent a test utility from quietly becoming an identity system. A practical retention and access model Separate the data plane from the evidence plane: Data plane: the temporary inbox and message body, accessible only to the test worker. Evidence plane: a small JSON receipt with correlation ID, delivery state, elapsed time, and a redacted failure reason. The receipt should be enough to answer “Did delivery happen?” and “Where did it wait?” without answering “What did the user receive?” If debugging needs more, make the expansion deliberate, time-limited, and visible in the run record. For flaky tests, Playwright traces for flaky email tests show why a timeline can be more useful than saving every message. The same principle applies to scheduled jobs: self-explaining cron runs make the outcome inspectable without preserving unrelated inputs. Make failures useful without keeping everything A test harness can emit a compact receipt like this: { "correlation_id" : "ci-1842-verify" , "mailbox_scope" : "worker-7" , "message_seen" : true , "delivery_ms" : 842 , "token_checked" : true , "body_retained" : false } The message_seen and delivery_ms fields help distinguish a provider delay from an application bug. token_checked confirms the assertion without printing the token. When the test fail, the harness can attach a redacted subject and the last polling event, then delete the inbox as part of cleanup. Cleanup should be defensive, not aspirational. Put it in a finally block, make deletion idempotent, and record cleanup failure separately from the original assertion. A small ledger make retries understandable: created, message observed, assertion passed, deleted. It also makes a leak visible when deletion did not happen. Checklist for the next review Ask these questions in the next email-test review: Does each parallel test have an isolated mailbox scope? Are verification tokens absent from ordinary logs and traces? Is the default retention shorter than the investigation window? Can an engineer diagnose timing without opening the message body? Does cleanup run after assertion failures and cancellations? Are screenshots and CI artifacts covered by the same policy? The goal is not to make testing slower or less observable. It is to make observability proportional. A privacy budget gives the team a shared tradeoff: retain the smallest evidence that explains the behavior, and require a reason before retaining anything more. That small boundary usually improves reliability too. Fewer shared inboxes means fewer cross-test races, fewer misleading retries, and less uncertainty about which message belongs to which run. The test become easier to trust because its evidence has a clear owner and an intentional lifetime.

title: Free HTTP Status Code Checker: Check Any URL's Status in Seconds
author: Vulnerability Tools
summary: Every time a browser or search engine requests a web page, the server answers with an HTTP status code. That three-digit code is a quick health signal for the page. The main groups are easy to remember: 2xx codes mean success, so the page loaded as expected. 3xx codes mean a redirect, so the visitor is sent somewhere else. 4xx codes mean a client-side problem, such as a missing page. 5xx codes mean a server-side problem, so the server could not complete the request. Checking a status code matters because a page can look fine in one browser while returning an error, a redirect chain, or the wrong response to search engines. A quick check helps you spot broken links, faulty redirects, and server errors before visitors or customers do. Try the free http status code checker to check any URL's status in seconds.

title: How to Fix 429 Too Many Requests in Laravel: Throttle and Rate Limiting Done Right
author: Ayesha
summary: You push to production, traffic grows, and suddenly your logs fill with 429 Too Many Requests in Laravel. Legitimate users see "Too Many Attempts", your mobile app starts failing, and your first instinct is to just turn the throttle off. That fixes it for a day. Then the bots find the endpoint, and you are debugging a very different problem at 3 a.m. This guide walks through every real cause of the 429 Too Many Requests error in Laravel, how to diagnose which one is biting you, and working code that fixes it without leaving your app unprotected. Everything below is tested against Laravel 11 and 12, where the api throttle middleware and named rate limiters work the same way. What the 429 Error Actually Means in Laravel The 429 Too Many Requests response comes from Laravel's throttle middleware. Every request that passes through it gets counted against a named limit — for example, 60 requests per minute. When the count for a key exceeds the limit, Laravel throws a ThrottleRequestsException and responds with 429. The important part is the key. Laravel counts attempts per key, and that key is built from the limiter you configured: usually the user's ID for logged-in users, or the IP address for guests. Most 429 Too Many Requests problems in Laravel are not about traffic being too high — they are about the key or the limiter being wrong. Every 429 response also carries a Retry-After header telling the client how many seconds to wait. If your custom error handling drops that header, API clients have no way to back off gracefully, and they hammer the endpoint again the moment they retry. Cause 1 — The Default API Throttle Is Too Strict Fresh Laravel apps ship with the api limiter set to 60 requests per minute per user or IP. That is fine for a toy project. A real dashboard with auto-refresh, polling, or a chatty mobile client can burn through 60 requests in seconds. Diagnose it first. Before changing anything, confirm the throttle middleware is actually attached to the route you think it is: php artisan route:list -v | grep throttle If the 429 responses carry an X-RateLimit-Remaining header that bottoms out at exactly 60, you are hitting the default api limiter. The fix is to define your own limiter with a sane budget instead of accepting the default. In Laravel 11 and 12, you define named limiters in your application's bootstrap: use Illuminate\Http\Request ; use Illuminate\Support\Facades\RateLimiter ; use Illuminate\Cache\RateLimiting\Limit ; // app/Providers/AppServiceProvider.php (or bootstrap/app.php) RateLimiter::for('api', function (Request $request) { return Limit::perMinute(300)->by($request->user()?->id ?: $request->ip()); }); This raises the budget to 300 per minute and, crucially, keys it on the user ID when someone is logged in. IP-keyed limits are dangerous for authenticated users: one office behind a NAT gateway shares a single IP, and five employees can exhaust a guest budget before any one of them looks abusive. Cause 2 — Two Endpoints Sharing One Limiter Inline limits like throttle:60,1 are easy to write and easy to regret. When you apply throttle:api to two different endpoints, both draw from the same budget. A webhook receiver and your search endpoint should never share a limit — one bursty integration drains the budget and the other starts 429-ing real users. The fix is one named limiter per behavior: RateLimiter :: for ( 'webhooks' , fn ( Request $request ) => Limit :: perMinute ( 600 ) -> by ( $request -> ip ())); RateLimiter::for('search', fn (Request $request) => Limit::perMinute(120)->by($request->user()?->id ?: $request->ip())); Route :: post ( '/webhooks/stripe' , [ WebhookController :: class , 'store' ]) -> middleware ( 'throttle:webhooks' ); Route::get('/search', [SearchController::class, 'index']) ->middleware('throttle:search'); This is the same isolation principle behind good API design: if you are building endpoints that third parties will hit at unpredictable rates, it pays to design them as a proper custom REST API from the start ( https://webixyhub.com/blog/custom-rest-api-development-cost-hiring-guide ) — isolated limits, versioned routes, and documented Retry-After behavior included. Cause 3 — Behind a Proxy, Every Request Has the Same IP This is the most common 429 Too Many Requests cause in production Laravel apps and the least obvious. When your app sits behind a load balancer, Cloudflare, or a reverse proxy, every request arrives from the proxy's IP. If your limiter keys on IP, all of your traffic — every user, every bot — counts as one person. The symptom: 429s spike immediately after a deploy or a traffic surge, the X-Forwarded-For header looks fine, but the throttled IP in your logs is always your proxy. The fix is to tell Laravel which proxies to trust. In Laravel 11+, add this to your bootstrap: -> withMiddleware ( function ( Middleware $middleware ) { $middleware -> trustProxies ( at : [ '*' ]); }) In production, never use at: ['*'] blindly — list your actual proxy addresses or CIDR ranges so clients cannot spoof X-Forwarded-For. Trusting the right proxies restores the real client IP, and your per-IP limits start working the way you intended. Cause 4 — File Cache Across Multiple Servers Laravel's throttle middleware stores its counters in the cache. If CACHE_DRIVER is set to file and you run two or more app servers, each server counts independently. Your effective limit is the configured limit multiplied by the number of servers, and worse, counters are never shared, so behavior looks random: a request fails on server A and succeeds on server B. The fix: use Redis (or Memcached) as the cache driver in any environment with more than one server: CACHE_DRIVER = redis With Redis the counters are atomic, fast, and shared across all servers. This one config change turns your rate limit from an estimate into an actual guarantee. Cause 5 — The throttleApi Error on Every Request In Laravel 11+, if you enable the api throttle with a named limiter that you never defined — for example, calling $middleware->throttleApi() and then attaching throttle:api to routes without a RateLimiter::for('api') definition — every API request 429s or errors from the first call. The symptom is unmistakable: a brand-new user makes one request and gets 429. The fix is to always define the limiter you reference. If you do not need per-user nuance, the simplest correct definition is: RateLimiter :: for ( 'api' , fn ( Request $request ) => Limit :: perMinute ( 60 )); No reference to a limiter anywhere means no mystery errors. Run php artisan route:list -v after wiring everything up and read the middleware column line by line. Cause 6 — Login and Auth Routes Keyed Wrong Auth endpoints deserve their own strict limit, keyed on more than just the email. A common setup limits logins per email, but then one attacker brute-forcing a single account burns through legitimate users' budgets, or worse, the lockout becomes a tool for denying real users access. A robust login limiter keys on the email plus the IP, and the whole flow clears the counter on success so a legitimate user starts fresh: public function login ( Request $request ) { $key = 'login:' . $request -> ip () . '|' . strtolower ( $request -> input ( 'email' )); if ( RateLimiter :: tooManyAttempts ( $key , 5 )) { return response () -> json ([ 'message' => 'Too many attempts. Please try again later.' , 'retry_after' => RateLimiter :: availableIn ( $key ), ], 429 ); } if ( ! Auth :: attempt ( $request -> only ( 'email' , 'password' ))) { RateLimiter :: hit ( $key , 60 ); return response () -> json ([ 'message' => 'Invalid credentials.' ], 401 ); } RateLimiter :: clear ( $key ); $request -> session () -> regenerate (); return response () -> json ([ 'message' => 'Authenticated.' ]); } Four methods do all the work here: RateLimiter::hit records an attempt, tooManyAttempts checks the count, clear resets it after a successful login, and availableIn returns the seconds until the limit resets so you can feed a honest Retry-After to the client. Never reveal how many attempts were made or whether the account exists — a generic message plus retry timing keeps brute-force attackers from enumerating users. Apply the same discipline to password resets, registration, OTP resends, and email verification: these are the endpoints bots actually attack. Handling 429 Gracefully Instead of Swallowing It Whatever you do, keep the Retry-After header in your 429 responses. If you customize the exception rendering, pass the headers through: use Illuminate\Http\Exceptions\ThrottleRequestsException ; public function render($request, Throwable $exception) { if ($exception instanceof ThrottleRequestsException) { Log::warning('Rate limit exceeded', [ 'ip' => $request->ip(), 'url' => $request->url(), ]); return response()->json([ 'message' => 'Too many requests. Please slow down and try again.', ], 429, $exception->getHeaders()); } return parent::render($request, $exception); } Logging every 429 with the IP and URL gives you the evidence trail you need. When a legitimate integration starts failing, you will see the pattern in minutes instead of guessing. And on the client side, respect the header: exponential backoff on 429 and 5xx responses is the difference between a retry that works and a retry storm. Testing Your Limits Before You Ship Do not trust a limiter you have never triggered. The cheapest verification is a curl loop from two machines against your real environment — your local setup cannot reproduce proxy IPs, shared caches, or real client behavior: for i in $( seq 1 70 ) ; do curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code} %{header_json} \n " \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN " \ https://webixyhub.com/api/search?q = demo done | sort | uniq -c You are looking for the first 60 responses to be 200 and the 61st onward to be 429 with a Retry-After header present. If 429s arrive early, your key is wrong (check trusted proxies). If they never arrive, your limiter is not attached or your cache driver is array in a real environment. The 429 Checklist One named limiter per behavior, never shared across unrelated endpoints. Limits keyed on user ID for authenticated traffic, IP only for guests. Trusted proxies configured with real addresses before launch, not after the first incident. Redis or another shared cache driver in production. Auth endpoints limited on email plus IP, with the counter cleared on successful login. Retry-After preserved in every custom 429 response. And a curl test against the real environment before you call it done. Rate limiting is one of those invisible engineering decisions that separates a side project from production software — like fixing the Stripe webhook signature verification flow ( https://webixyhub.com/blog/fix-stripe-webhook-signature-verification-failed-laravel ) or the N+1 query problem in Laravel ( https://webixyhub.com/blog/fix-n1-query-problem-laravel-eager-loading ), it only matters when it breaks, and then it matters a lot. If rate limiting, API design, or a tricky Laravel bug is eating your week, I can take it off your plate. Reach out through https://webixyhub.com and tell me what is breaking — or see how I evaluate Laravel expertise when teams ask me to vet one ( https://webixyhub.com/blog/hire-laravel-developer-guide ).

title: Are You a Web Developer or a Browser Expert? 7 Tests I Failed Building a Photo Editor That Never Uploads Your Photos
author: Akhouri Anmol Kumar
summary: Description: On-device AI, WASM threads, target-size compression, inpainting and 3D LUTs in a single HTML file. 7 real lessons from building APIC Web. Most web developers can build a form, fetch an API and center a div. Browser experts know what the browser refuses to do, what happens on a phone instead of your laptop, and how to ship real software with no server at all . I found out which one I was while building APIC Web : a free photo editor, background remover, object remover, converter and compressor where your photos never leave your device . No upload queue, no backend, and the whole thing is one HTML file hosted on GitHub Pages. Every test below is a real bug or design decision from that build. Score yourself honestly. 👇 Test 1: Why did my AI step silently never finish on phones? APIC runs AI models in the browser with ONNX Runtime Web (WebAssembly). Multi-threaded WASM needs SharedArrayBuffer , and that needs special response headers (COOP/COEP). A plain static host like GitHub Pages doesn't send them, so crossOriginIsolated is false . On desktop, the runtime usually degrades gracefully. On phones it often doesn't, and the AI step just hangs with no error. The fix was to stop relying on the fallback: // Static hosts can't send COOP/COEP, so threads aren't available. // Force the one configuration that behaves the same everywhere. ort . env . wasm . numThreads = 1 ; ort . env . wasm . proxy = false ; const session = await ort . InferenceSession . create ( modelBytes , { executionProviders : [ ' wasm ' ], enableCpuMemArena : false , enableMemPattern : false , }); Where headers are available, APIC checks self.crossOriginIsolated before asking for more than one thread. Developer: "It works on my laptop." Expert: knows that "falls back gracefully" is a claim to test on a real phone, not a promise. Test 2: Can you tell a slow download from a dead one? APIC's AI models are big: 5 MB (Lite), 44 MB (Fast), 176 MB (Maximum) for background removal, and about 208 MB for the highest-quality object remover. A fixed 30-second timeout would kill every slow phone connection. So the timeout is stall-based : abort only if no bytes arrive for 40 seconds . A huge model on bad Wi-Fi is allowed to take as long as it needs. A dead link is not. After that it goes into the Cache API so the second run is instant: const CACHE = ' apic-models-v1 ' ; const cache = await caches . open ( CACHE ); let hit = await cache . match ( url ); if ( hit ) return hit . arrayBuffer (); // cached: no download const bytes = await downloadWithStallTimeout ( url ); // abort only if the stream goes quiet await cache . put ( url , new Response ( bytes )); // wrapped in try/catch: private mode & quota can fail return bytes ; And if a model can't load at all, the tool steps down instead of failing: Ultra (LaMa) → MI-GAN → a quick patch fill. Developer: fetch() with a timeout. Expert: measures progress, caches the result, and always has a plan B. Test 3: Can your app hit "under 200 KB" without guessing? Upload forms say "max 200 KB" and users play quality-slider roulette. APIC's Compress tool does a binary search on JPEG quality instead: async function findQualityForTarget ( canvas , targetBytes ) { let lo = 0.05 , hi = 0.98 , best = null ; for ( let i = 0 ; i < 7 ; i ++ ) { const mid = ( lo + hi ) / 2 ; const blob = await toBlob ( canvas , ' image/jpeg ' , mid ); if ( blob . size <= targetBytes ) { best = { blob , q : mid }; lo = mid ; } // fits: try higher quality else { hi = mid ; } // too big: go lower } return best ; } Seven encodes find the highest quality that still fits. If even the lowest quality is too big, APIC shrinks the image by about 20% and searches again, up to 8 times. If it still can't make it, it tells you the real size instead of pretending. Developer: quality = 0.7 and hope. Expert: turns a guess into a search and is honest when the answer is "can't". Test 4: Why did my transparent PNG turn black as a JPEG? JPEG has no alpha channel. When a canvas with transparent pixels is encoded as JPEG, those pixels come out black . After background removal (which creates lots of transparency), that's a nasty surprise. The fix is to paint white first, then draw the image on top: function flattenToWhite ( src ) { const out = document . createElement ( ' canvas ' ); out . width = src . width ; out . height = src . height ; const ctx = out . getContext ( ' 2d ' ); ctx . fillStyle = ' #fff ' ; ctx . fillRect ( 0 , 0 , out . width , out . height ); ctx . drawImage ( src , 0 , 0 ); return out ; } APIC also tells you which formats keep transparency (PNG, WebP) and which don't, right in the Convert panel. Developer: assumes a canvas is just pixels. Expert: knows every output format has rules about alpha. Test 5: Do you process the whole image, or only what changed? Removing an object means running an inpainting model (LaMa, a Fourier-convolution network, or the lighter MI-GAN). LaMa works on a fixed 512×512 window, so feeding it a 12-megapixel photo would be slow and blurry. APIC only processes the area around your brush : Take a region around the mask (at least 512 native pixels when the photo allows). Run the model on just that crop. Feather the edge with box blurs, colour-match the fill to its surroundings, and re-add film grain so it doesn't look "too clean". Paste it back. Small edit, small compute, and the rest of your photo is untouched . Developer: runs the model on the full image. Expert: shrinks the problem first, then blends the result back so nobody can see the seam. Test 6: Can you export your whole colour grade as a .cube LUT? APIC has curves, an 8-band HSL mixer and 3-way colour grading. People wanted to use those grades in DaVinci Resolve or Premiere. A .cube file is a 3D lookup table: for every input colour, what colour comes out. The trick: you don't need to reverse-engineer your pipeline. Feed an identity grid of colours through the same pixel function, and write down what comes out: const N = 33 ; // 33×33×33 lattice const buf = new Uint8ClampedArray ( N * N * N * 4 ); let i = 0 ; for ( let b = 0 ; b < N ; b ++ ) for ( let g = 0 ; g < N ; g ++ ) for ( let r = 0 ; r < N ; r ++ ) { // red changes fastest, as .cube requires buf [ i ++ ] = Math . round ( r / ( N - 1 ) * 255 ); buf [ i ++ ] = Math . round ( g / ( N - 1 ) * 255 ); buf [ i ++ ] = Math . round ( b / ( N - 1 ) * 255 ); buf [ i ++ ] = 255 ; } processPixels ( buf , gradeWithoutSpatialEffects ); // same code that edits your photo const lines = [ ' TITLE "APIC grade" ' , ' LUT_3D_SIZE 33 ' , ' DOMAIN_MIN 0.0 0.0 0.0 ' , ' DOMAIN_MAX 1.0 1.0 1.0 ' , '' ]; for ( let j = 0 ; j < buf . length ; j += 4 ) lines . push ( ` ${( buf [ j ] / 255 ). toFixed ( 6 )} ${( buf [ j + 1 ] / 255 ). toFixed ( 6 )} ${( buf [ j + 2 ] / 255 ). toFixed ( 6 )} ` ); One catch: a LUT can only hold colour operations. Clarity, sharpen, vignette and grain depend on neighbouring pixels, so they're excluded and the UI says so. Developer: exports a screenshot of the look. Expert: samples the function itself. Test 7: Why does your resized image look soft? ctx . drawImage ( img , 0 , 0 , smallW , smallH ); // one big jump: soft, aliased Shrinking a large image in one drawImage call looks muddy. APIC's Resize tool halves the image step by step until it's within 2× of the target, then does one final pass: function highQualityResize ( src , targetW , targetH ) { let cur = src , w = src . width , h = src . height ; while ( w > targetW * 2 || h > targetH * 2 ) { const nw = Math . max ( targetW , Math . round ( w / 2 )); const nh = Math . max ( targetH , Math . round ( h / 2 )); const step = document . createElement ( ' canvas ' ); step . width = nw ; step . height = nh ; const c = step . getContext ( ' 2d ' ); c . imageSmoothingEnabled = true ; c . imageSmoothingQuality = ' high ' ; c . drawImage ( cur , 0 , 0 , nw , nh ); cur = step ; w = nw ; h = nh ; } // ...then one last high-quality pass onto the exact target size } Developer: drawImage once and move on. Expert: knows the order of operations changes the result. Bonus: How do you ship a Web Worker inside a single HTML file? No build step, no separate worker.js . APIC keeps the worker's source as a string, turns it into a Blob and starts it from a Blob URL: const SRC = `/* worker code as a string */` ; const worker = new Worker ( URL . createObjectURL ( new Blob ([ SRC ], { type : ' application/javascript ' })) ); Heavy inpainting runs off the main thread, and the whole app is still one file you can host anywhere. Try it yourself APIC is built by Akhouri Systems . It runs in your browser, and your images are never uploaded. The only thing the browser downloads is the AI model files (from Hugging Face), cached after the first run. Being upfront about the trade-offs: editing needs no account, you sign in with one tap on Google only when you export , and the web version shows one small banner ad to stay free. The offline PC app has none. App What it is Lessons it proves Get it 🖼️ APIC Web Edit, pro colour tools, remove objects, remove backgrounds with AI, resize, convert, compress, 15-network social presets, batch ZIP Tests 1-7 Open APIC Web 💻 APIC for PC Windows version, runs fully offline, no account The desktop twin Download (zip) If you're learning how the browser works outside a tutorial, open it, drop a photo, then open DevTools and see what's going on under the hood. That's the fastest way I know to level up. Your score 0-2 tests known: You're a web developer . Great start, now break something on a real phone. 3-5: Solid. You've shipped something real. 6-7: You're a browser expert . Come argue with me in the comments. Which test did you fail first? Mine was [the AI step that worked on desktop and silently hung on phones]. Tell me yours below 👇

title: DeadLock: The Ghost in the Local Machine 🎃👻
author: Sakeena Patel
summary: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine. What I Built Imagine you’re locked in a server room after hours. The lights are dead. The terminals are humming. But the monster haunting the dark isn't a zombie or a vampire—it's a silent, insidious AI engineering bug. DeadLock is a local, browser-based puzzle game where your weapons are debugging skills and your enemies are real-world AI failures. Across 5 eerie levels and 10 distinct challenges, you inspect a Ai engineering challenges edit it right in your browser, and hit Compile and attack. Treat 🍫: Your code passes the assertions. You survive. Trick: Your code fails. No points, no escape, try again. A flawless run nets you 50 points. Need help? You can summon the ghost in the machine for a hint—powered entirely by a local open-weight model—at the steep cost of 5 points per clue. Two hints max for the whole game. Choose wisely. Demo DeadLock_Demo.mp4 - Google Drive drive.google.com Code dataWizard7957 / deadlock DeadLock DeadLock is a local, browser-based game for practicing AI-engineering tasks. Players repair short Python functions covering prompts, sampling settings, context limits, retrieval, and evaluation. The puzzles run entirely on the machine. Hints, when used, are generated by a local model through Ollama. How to play The game has five levels, and each level has two challenges. A challenge is a broken function. Edit the code and choose Compile and attack . A correct fix is a Treat . Clearing both challenges in a level awards 10 points. An incorrect fix is a Trick . The score does not change, and the challenge stays open. A perfect run with no hints, is 50 points. The player has two hints for the whole game. Each hint costs 5 points and requests a short clue from the local model. The game remains playable if Ollama is not running; the hint then reports… View on GitHub How I Built It The core gameplay loop is completely offline-first. To ensure the game stays snappy and playable even if your local LLM server is offline, the puzzle verification doesn't use an AI model at all. Every player fix is instantly validated via deterministic Python assertions running locally on the machine. The open-source AI piece is reserved for the atmosphere. When you burn a hint, dungeon/dm.py sends a minimalist prompt directly to a local Ollama It explicitly ignores proxy settings to ensure local routing stays local. It optimizes for gemma2:2b if installed, handling cold starts gracefully. It asks the model strictly for a clue, never the raw solution. The frontend uses Streamlit to create a seamless, retro-arcade coding experience right in your browser. Why Does Open Innovation Matter? When you play DeadLock, you are writing snippets of real AI systems: prompt architecture, sampling parameters, retrieval strategies. If this were built on a commercial chat API, every keystroke and hint request would siphon your code off to someone else's servers, running up a token bill while leaking code architecture. A local, open-weight model flips the script: Absolute Privacy: Your code never leaves your hardware. Zero Marginal Cost: Hints cost game points, not API dollars. Unfiltered Tone: The Halloween flavor and system prompt live locally, untouched by corporate safety filters or external policy classifiers. Resilience: If Ollama drops connection, the puzzles still work. The ghost is optional. The engineering is absolute. The Spirit of It The magic of DeadLock lives in the space right beneath the code editor. When you click attack, the machine responds instantly with either a Treat 🍫 or a Trick. There are no long-winded paragraphs explaining the bug above the code. You read the syntax, you spot the flaw, you fix the logic, and the machine either opens the door or locks you out. Pure logic meets midnight atmosphere. Prize Categories Best Use of Gemma Used Gemma as hint—powered entirely by a local open weight model. 2.Best Use of ElevenLabs It was used for recording voiceover for demo.

title: Cisco Gave One Engineer Unlimited AI Tokens to Rewrite 98%
author: Max Quimby
summary: Cisco president Jeetu Patel found Padmanabhan Krishnamurthy five levels below him in the org chart during a visit to the company's San Francisco office. Krishnamurthy is 27, the former CEO of translation startup EzDubs (acquired by Cisco in 2025), and was — in Patel's words — "buried away doing something unstrategic." Patel pulled him out and gave him a mandate: take a two-person team, unlimited AI tokens, and rewrite 98% of Cisco's legacy codebase within 24 months . The instruction was simple: "go nuts." 📖 Read the full version with charts and embedded sources on AgentConn → Read the original Fortune article → The story hit Fortune on October 30, 2026, and the internet split cleanly down the middle. Hacker News gave it 282 points and 330 comments , mostly bullish — commenters reported their own 50,000-line migrations finishing in a week. Reddit's r/technology gave it 12,933 upvotes and 1,895 comments , mostly skeptical — a "PR stunt" that conveniently eliminates the need for entry-level engineers. That split is the story. Not whether coding agents can translate syntax — they can, and have been doing it reliably for months. The real question is whether a $429 billion enterprise can reorganize itself to accept, review, test, and trust millions of lines of AI-generated code. That is an organizational problem wearing an engineering costume. ℹ️ The Cisco Experiment at a Glance Engineer: Padmanabhan Krishnamurthy, 27, ex-CEO of EzDubs Mandate: Rewrite 98% of Cisco's legacy codebase Timeline: 4-week proof of concept, 24-month full execution Team size: 2 people Resources: Unlimited AI tokens Budget context: Cisco is a $429B company with 85% of engineers already using AI tools The Case For: Language Translation Is AI's Sweet Spot The HN thread reads like a support group for engineers who have already done what Cisco is proposing. The top comment is concrete: "We just recently used Claude Code to port an old ColdFusion site to Java Spring and it went amazingly well. It's around 50K lines of Java, one of our engineers did it in his spare time over about a week, using the $200/mo Claude plan." View the full HN discussion → This is not an isolated anecdote. The second-most-upvoted comment makes the structural argument: "Translating from one language/platform to another is something AI is very very good at, so this sounds like a good use of it, bonus points if they create a comprehensive test suite first." The logic holds. Code translation is a bounded problem with well-defined inputs and outputs. Unlike open-ended feature development, you know what the code is supposed to do — it is already doing it. The agent's job is to preserve behavior while changing syntax and architecture. This is closer to compilation than creativity. Nick Hodges, the former Delphi product manager, made this case explicitly in an InfoWorld opinion piece two weeks before the Cisco story broke. He argues that Joel Spolsky's famous 2000 warning against rewrites — that legacy code holds hard-won knowledge, and rewrites discard it — no longer applies. Coding agents can read the spaghetti, trace the tangled procedures, and carry the edge-case knowledge forward. His estimate: agents could handle "about 98% of a modernization, finished in a person-month or two." Read the InfoWorld article → Cisco's own track record supports the bullish read. Patel told the Financial Times that one product is now written entirely by AI , with no human-written lines. The company has saved over 1,500 engineering hours per month using OpenAI's Codex. And he predicts 70% of Cisco's product portfolio will be fully AI-generated by the end of 2027 . The Case Against: Organizational Antibodies Kill More Rewrites Than Bad Code Reddit saw the same Fortune article and reached the opposite conclusion. The r/technology thread's dominant read: this is a job-elimination narrative dressed in innovation language. View the Reddit discussion → The skeptics are not wrong to be suspicious. The Fortune article opens by noting that 40% of UK employers plan to hire fewer graduates because AI can do the work more cheaply. Patel's language reinforces this — he wants to hire Gen Z engineers specifically because they are "native" to AI tools and will "challenge the status quo." One cynical reading: a 27-year-old with unlimited tokens is cheaper than 200 senior engineers with institutional knowledge. The same day, a 466-point HN thread argued that AI is not replacing SREs — it is deskilling them. The concern is not that AI cannot write code, but that organizations will mistake AI output for verified output and erode the engineering expertise needed to catch what the agent gets wrong. View the HN thread on AI deskilling → But the deeper objection is not about labor politics. It is about the organizational machinery required to absorb a rewrite. Joel Spolsky's 2000 essay was not really about code quality. It was about the invisible specifications embedded in a running system . Every bug fix is a learned lesson. Every edge case is a customer conversation. Every weird conditional is a compliance requirement that nobody documented. Rewriting the code does not just risk losing those lessons — it requires the organization to re-learn them, usually in production. ⚠️ The Contrarian Take Cisco's "98% rewrite" may be the right engineering decision and still fail as an organizational one. The bottleneck is not code generation — it is code review, testing, and institutional trust. A two-person team generating millions of lines of code creates a verification crisis: who reviews it? Who signs off that the edge cases survived translation? A 50K-line ColdFusion port done "in spare time" is a different beast from a fleet-wide rewrite of a $429B company's production systems. This is not theoretical. Spotify's Honk agent has merged over 1,500 AI-generated pull requests and reports 60-90% time savings on migrations. But Spotify's own post-mortem is revealing: the success created a new bottleneck in PR review . At QCon London 2026, the team reported that what used to take three months to hit 1,000 merged PRs now takes ten days — but the review queue exploded. Read the Spotify Engineering post → 200OK Solutions tested five AI coding agents on a legacy codebase and found that every single agent made at least one change that would have caused a production issue if merged without review . Claude Code scored high on reasoning but weak on undocumented business rules. This is exactly the failure mode Spolsky predicted — the knowledge that lives in the code but not in any spec. The Evidence From the Field The Cisco experiment does not exist in a vacuum. A pattern is emerging across enterprise engineering: Cisco's own numbers: 85% of engineers already use AI tools daily. One product shipped with 100% AI-generated code. Over 1,500 engineering hours saved monthly via Codex. The 98% rewrite target builds on proven tooling, not speculative capability. Spotify's Honk: 1,500+ PRs merged, 60-90% time savings on dataset migrations. The background coding agent now handles language modernization (Java records), breaking-change upgrades, UI component migrations, and config changes. But it took a purpose-built fleet orchestration system and custom review tooling to make it work. Meanwhile, another HN post about "building an AI-native engineering org" was called out for vanity metrics — LOC, tokens, releases — with no revenue data. The community consensus: output metrics without quality gates are marketing. View the HN thread on AI-native engineering → The Sonar reality check: Sonar's 2026 research shows that LOC output is up 2,450% with AI agents, but actual releases only increased 30%. The productivity multiplier on raw output does not translate linearly to shipped product. And 96% of developers say they do not fully trust AI-generated code — which means every line needs review. The 10x PRs, 1x reviewers problem is now the industry's central bottleneck. IBM Technology's warning: IBM's recent analysis of AI exposing legacy code makes a complementary point: AI is forcing teams back into abandoned legacy systems before hidden dependency risks bite. The push to rewrite is not just about modernization — it is about risk management for code nobody has touched in years. The $30 Billion Question: Who Owns the Risk? The legacy code modernization market is now estimated at $30 billion and growing. Anthropic has committed $100 million to a partner network focused on code modernization. IBM's watsonx Code Assistant for Z converts COBOL to Java. GitHub Copilot has launched a dedicated migration workflow. Morgan Stanley built an in-house tool because commercial solutions "lacked expertise in company-specific legacy languages." The common pattern: every enterprise that has successfully used agents for migration built custom tooling around the agent , not the agent alone. Spotify built Honk and Fleet Management. Morgan Stanley built a proprietary translation layer. The agent is necessary but not sufficient — the harness is the moat . This is what makes Cisco's experiment genuinely interesting. A two-person team with unlimited tokens is not a production organization. It is a proof of concept. The four-week trial will show whether AI can translate Cisco's legacy code. The 24-month execution will show whether Cisco's organization can absorb the output. ℹ️ What the Legacy Rewrite Market Looks Like in 2026 Market size: $30B+ for legacy code modernization Active vendors: Anthropic ($100M partner fund), IBM (watsonx Code Assistant), GitHub (Copilot migration CLI), OpenAI (Codex) Enterprise evidence: Spotify (1,500+ PRs), Cisco (product shipped 100% AI), Morgan Stanley (custom tooling) Key finding: Every successful migration at scale used custom harness tooling, not raw agent output Failure rate: 60% of enterprise AI agent pilots fail to scale past pilot stage What This Means for Teams Building with Agents If you are an engineering leader evaluating coding agents for legacy migration, the Cisco story offers three lessons: 1. Start with translation, not creation. The HN commenters are right — language-to-language migration is AI's sweet spot. It is bounded, testable, and does not require the agent to invent new architecture. Your first agent project should be a code translation, not a greenfield build. 2. Build the review infrastructure first. Spotify learned this the hard way: the bottleneck moves from code generation to code review faster than you expect. Before you give an agent unlimited tokens, build the quality gates that will process its output. Automated test generation, diff review tooling, and merge approval workflows are the prerequisite, not the afterthought. 3. Measure organizational absorption, not engineering output. The 2,450% increase in LOC output is meaningless if releases only go up 30%. The metric that matters is not "how much code did the agent write" but "how much code did the organization ship, verify, and trust." Track merged-and-deployed, not generated. The Cisco experiment will be a fascinating case study over the next 24 months. If Krishnamurthy's two-person team actually rewrites 98% of a $429B company's legacy code, it will be the most dramatic demonstration of coding agent ROI in enterprise history. If it stalls — and the Reddit skeptics are betting it will — it will confirm that the agent was never the bottleneck. The organization was. Either way, the debate is settled on one point: legacy code migration is now the default first use case for enterprise coding agents. The question is no longer "can AI rewrite code?" It is "can your company handle it when it does?" Originally published at AgentConn

title: Originality.ai vs NeuronWriter: Which Tool Fits Content Teams?
author: Rennie Hoffman
summary: ⚡ Executive Verdict: Originality.ai vs NeuronWriter (2026) Originality.ai Advantage: Originality.ai stands out for Teams evaluating AI SEO software and comparing official feature positioning. NeuronWriter Advantage: NeuronWriter is superior for Teams evaluating AI SEO software and comparing official feature positioning. Workflow & Usability: Originality.ai provides faster setup and lighter onboarding, whereas NeuronWriter accommodates more complex multi-seat pipelines. Which One to Pick: Choose Originality.ai for speed and solo workflows; select NeuronWriter if your organization requires team-wide scaling. Introduction Originality.ai and NeuronWriter are both relevant to content teams, but they support different stages of production. Originality.ai focuses on AI detection, plagiarism, fact checking, readability, and related editorial analysis. NeuronWriter focuses on semantic content optimization, AI-assisted writing, AI monitoring, content planning, and integrations such as Google Search Console, WordPress, and Shopify on selected plans. This comparison uses official documentation checked on September 8, 2026. It is not a paid-account test. We did not measure rankings, detector accuracy, plagiarism recall, output quality, or citation performance. The short answer Choose NeuronWriter when the priority is planning and optimizing content for search and AI visibility. Choose Originality.ai when the priority is reviewing text for possible AI generation, copied wording, factual issues, or readability. If a team needs both, use NeuronWriter earlier in the workflow and Originality.ai as a separate QA layer. NeuronWriter: optimize and manage content NeuronWriter’s official pricing page lists content writer analyses, AI credits, AI-monitored questions, content planning, AI templates, content sharing, plagiarism checks, integrations, content management, and an API on higher plans. It also describes projects or folders as a way to organize work. That makes NeuronWriter relevant to SEO writers, small agencies, and teams that need a semantic brief, an optimization workspace, and repeatable content operations. The product can help answer what a page should cover and how the team might organize drafts and monitoring. The limitation is evidence discipline. An optimization score does not establish that a claim is true, that a source is authoritative, or that a page will rank. Writers still need a source packet, editorial policy, and final human review. Originality.ai: inspect the draft Originality.ai’s official pricing page describes AI detection, plagiarism checks, readability, fact checking, grammar, site scanning, API access, report sharing, and team seats. It uses credits for some checks and states that AI and plagiarism scans consume credits differently. This is useful when the editorial decision is about risk or review status. A publisher can flag a draft for deeper source checking, compare suspected copied wording, or apply a consistent disclosure and review policy. It is not a search-intent or content-brief tool. Detection must be handled carefully. The official detector-reliability discussion says no detector is perfect. A score is a signal for investigation, not proof of authorship. Review revision history, citations, source notes, and the writer’s process before taking a consequential action. Pricing NeuronWriter’s public pricing page lists Bronze at $23 per month monthly or $19 per month with annual billing, Silver at $45 or $37, Gold at $69 or $57, Platinum at $93 or $77, and Diamond at $117 or $97 at the time checked. The plans differ by projects, analyses, AI credits, monitored questions, sharing, integrations, and advanced features. Originality.ai’s pricing page lists Pro at $14.95 monthly or $12.95 on annual billing, and Enterprise at $179 monthly or $136.58 on annual billing at the time checked. It describes monthly credit pools, additional seats, scan history, and API access on relevant plans. The headline prices hide different consumption units. Model a month using content analyses, AI words, monitored questions, pages, words scanned, plagiarism checks, fact checks, seats, and API calls. Check the official website for the latest pricing. Pros and cons NeuronWriter’s strengths are search-oriented planning, semantic optimization, AI-assisted drafting, content organization, and selected CMS or analytics integrations. Its drawbacks are that more features require more setup, plan limits can be complex, and optimization guidance does not replace fact checking. Originality.ai’s strengths are focused text analysis, credit accounting, report sharing, team workflows, and API access. Its drawbacks are the possibility of false positives or overconfident interpretation, usage-based costs, and a narrower role in planning the actual page. A combined workflow Start with the reader and the query. Use NeuronWriter to create a brief, identify relevant coverage, draft or optimize the page, and preserve the sources that support each material claim. Do not write a sentence merely to satisfy a term or score. Then apply Originality.ai according to policy. Scan the final draft for the checks your team actually needs, record the date and document version, and route material flags to a reviewer. For a plagiarism flag, compare the wording and citation. For a fact flag, open the source. For an AI-detection flag, review process evidence rather than treating the score as authorship proof. After publication, keep the original draft, source packet, metadata, and review record. NeuronWriter’s monitoring or integration features can support a refresh process, while Originality.ai can be used again when a new draft or contribution needs QA. This separation keeps optimization and authorship questions from contaminating each other. Alternatives Surfer is an alternative for teams that want content audit and optimization workflows with a different product structure. Frase is relevant when research, SEO/GEO scoring, publishing, and content monitoring need to be connected. Grammarly or a human copy editor may be a better alternative when the problem is clarity and tone rather than search coverage. For AI detection and originality review, a documented editorial policy, source-checking process, and plagiarism-specific service may be more appropriate than a detector score alone. The right alternative depends on the risk and decision in front of the team. Final Verdict NeuronWriter is the better fit for content planning, semantic optimization, and AI-assisted SEO workflows. Originality.ai is the better fit for editorial analysis and review signals. Use NeuronWriter first and Originality.ai second only when both are needed, and keep source evidence, optimization metrics, and detector results as separate records. title: The golden set: 100 labelled examples as the acceptance test for an AI feature
author: Slava Kotenev
summary: If you ask three people whether an AI feature "works", you will get three answers, each based on the last few examples they happened to see. A golden set replaces opinions with a number: a fixed collection of real inputs with agreed correct answers, run every time something changes. About a hundred items is enough to start. Why a hundred With 100 items, one mistake moves the score by one point, and you can still read every failure by hand. That is the point of the first set: not statistical perfection, but a measurement the whole team can inspect. As the feature matures you grow it; you do not start with thousands. A caution on precision: with 100 items the uncertainty is wide. A 95% score can plausibly hide a true rate anywhere from roughly 89% to 98%. Treat it as a tripwire, not a guarantee, and say so in the acceptance document. What goes into it Sample from real data from the process, not from examples someone invented. Then deliberately cover: The typical case , in proportion to how common it is (most of the set). The boring variations : different phrasings, formats, languages, typos. Known hard cases : the pairs people confuse, the odd layouts. Things that must be refused or escalated : out-of-scope questions, missing fields, items the system should hand to a human. A few adversarial ones : instructions hidden in the input, empty input, absurdly long input. Tag each item with its category so you can report per-category results, not just one average that hides a weak spot. Who labels it The process owner, or someone they trust, decides the correct answer. Two people labelling independently, then discussing disagreements, finds the ambiguous items early. Ambiguity found at this stage is a requirements problem, and it is cheaper to fix now than after launch. How to use it Freeze it. The set is not training data. Never tune on it after you start reporting from it, or the score only reflects what you memorised. Run it on every change : a new prompt, a new model version, a new threshold. Write the pass bar before the first run , as a number per category. Example: "at least 95% correct on automated items, and every must-refuse item refused". Read the failures , all of them. Each one is either a bug, a labelling error, or a missing rule. Keep a changelog of scores per version so regressions are visible. A minimal runner is a few lines: def evaluate ( system , items ): results = [( it , system ( it [ " input " ])) for it in items ] ok = [ r for it , r in results if r [ " answer " ] == it [ " expected " ]] return len ( ok ) / len ( items ), [ it for it , r in results if r [ " answer " ] != it [ " expected " ]] Refresh it slowly Every month or so, add 10 to 20 fresh real items, especially ones that came out of the review queue as corrections. Retire items that no longer reflect the process. Keep a separate untouched holdout if you tune a lot. Takeaways Start with about 100 real, labelled items. Cover typical, hard, and must-refuse cases and tag them. Freeze it, write the pass bar first, run it on every change. Be honest about the uncertainty that comes with a small set. title: How to build your own salon booking app in Dubai (Arabic and English, no per-booking commission)
author: Mythex
summary: Spend ten minutes in any UAE salon owners' group and you'll see the same question every few weeks: "Which booking software do you use?" The replies split three ways. Some owners love a big marketplace app. Some complain about setup fees, per-booking commissions, or a booking page that doesn't look like their brand. And a surprising number admit they still take most bookings on WhatsApp and write them in a diary at reception. This guide is for the third and second groups. It walks through what a salon booking app actually needs, then builds one step by step with an AI app builder, using the exact prompts you'd type. At the end there's an honest section on what you give up compared with a ready-made salon platform, so you can decide which route fits your salon. What a salon in the Gulf actually needs from a booking app Before choosing any tool, write down how a booking moves through your salon today. For most small and mid-size salons in Dubai, Abu Dhabi, Riyadh or Doha it looks like this: The client finds you on Instagram, Google Maps or by word of mouth. They message to book , usually on WhatsApp, often in Arabic, sometimes in English, Russian or Tagalog. Reception checks who is free : which stylist, which chair or room, how long the service takes. The booking goes into a diary , a spreadsheet, or a shared calendar. Someone reminds the client the day before, if they remember. The client arrives , pays at the counter, and maybe books the next visit. The pain points are always in steps 2, 3 and 5: messages answered late, double bookings when two receptionists use different diaries, and no-shows because no reminder went out. So the minimum app is smaller than most software makes it look: A public booking page showing services, prices and durations, in Arabic and English. A slot picker that only shows times when the chosen stylist (or any stylist) is free. An admin screen for reception : today's bookings by stylist, with buttons to confirm, move or cancel. A client list with visit history and notes ("allergic to this product", "prefers Sara"). Reminders , at least a list of tomorrow's bookings that reception can message, or automatic messages if you connect a provider. Everything else (gift cards, packages, loyalty points, inventory) can come later. Step 1: describe your salon in one prompt In an AI app builder like Mythex you start by describing the app in plain language. Be specific about your services and how your salon works. The more real your description, the less you'll need to fix later. Here's the first prompt: A booking app for a ladies' beauty salon in Dubai. Arabic and English with a language switch, Arabic right-to-left. Public booking page: services with category, price in AED and duration (haircut 45 min AED 150, blow-dry 30 min AED 90, colour 120 min AED 450, manicure 45 min AED 100, pedicure 60 min AED 130). Client picks a service, then a stylist or "any available", then a free time slot, and enters name and phone number. Opening hours Saturday to Thursday 10:00–22:00, Friday 14:00–22:00. Admin page for reception: today's bookings grouped by stylist, confirm / reschedule / cancel, and a client list with visit history and notes. Mythex writes the code, creates a Postgres database for services, stylists, clients and bookings, and shows a live preview within a few minutes. Open the booking page in the preview and try to book something, as a client would. Step 2: fix what doesn't match how your salon works The first version is never exactly right, and that's fine. You keep refining by chat. Typical follow-ups for a salon: Each stylist only does some services. Nour does colour and blow-dry, Sara does haircut and blow-dry, Maria does nails only. Only show a stylist for services they do. Add a 15-minute cleaning buffer after every colour appointment. When a client books with "any available", assign the stylist with the fewest bookings that day. Add a "home service" option for manicure and pedicure with an area field (Dubai Marina, JLT, Downtown, Jumeirah) and AED 50 extra. After each change, book a test appointment again. Try the awkward cases on purpose: two people booking the same slot, a booking that runs past closing time, a Friday morning. Step 3: make the admin side useful for reception Reception is the person who will live in this app all day, so ask them what they need. Usually it's something like: On the admin page add a day view with one column per stylist and bookings as blocks, like a calendar. Let reception drag a booking to another time or stylist. Add a "walk-in" button that creates a booking for now with the first free stylist. Add a "Tomorrow" tab listing every booking with the client's phone number and a WhatsApp button that opens a pre-filled reminder message in Arabic or English, depending on the client's language. That last one is a practical trick. Fully automatic WhatsApp or SMS messages need a messaging provider account (and each message has a cost), but a one-click pre-filled WhatsApp link costs nothing and still cuts no-shows, because reception actually sends the reminders. If you later want automatic messages, you can ask the builder to connect a provider such as Twilio or the WhatsApp Business API using your own account keys. Step 4: protect the admin pages The booking page is public; the admin pages must not be. Ask for it explicitly: Only signed-in staff can open the admin pages. Add a staff login with email and password, and two roles: Owner (sees everything including revenue) and Reception (bookings and clients only). Mythex builds the sign-in with your app's own database. It isn't a separate login product, so test it: open the admin URL in a private window and check that it asks you to sign in. Step 5: publish it on your own domain When it works, publish. You get a public URL straight away, and you can connect your own domain (for example book.yoursalon.ae) from the project's domain settings. Put the link in your Instagram bio, your Google Maps profile and your WhatsApp Business auto-reply. That's where most Gulf salon clients will find it. If you want the app on clients' phones, the Pro plan can also turn the same app into an Android app (a download, or Google Play internal testing) and an iPhone app through TestFlight. These are your web screens wrapped as an app, not a fully native app, so for most salons the web booking link is enough to start. What you get, and the honest limits What you get: a booking app that's yours. Your branding, your services, Arabic and English, your domain, and your client data in your own database. No per-booking commission: you pay for the builder plan, not per appointment. When something changes (a new stylist, Ramadan hours, a new service), you describe the change and it's done. What you give up compared with a ready-made salon platform: No marketplace. Platforms like Fresha or Booksy also list you in their consumer app, which can bring new clients. Your own app only gets the clients you send to it. If most of your new clients come from a marketplace, keep it and use your own app for repeat clients. Payments need your own provider. Taking deposits online means connecting a payment provider account (Stripe, or a Gulf provider such as Tap or Telr) and asking the builder to add it. Not hard, but it's your account and their fees. Point-of-sale hardware and inventory aren't included out of the box. If you need a card terminal integration, a dedicated salon POS is still the easier choice. You are the one who maintains it. Changes are by chat, not code, but someone at the salon has to own the app. A sensible path for many salons is to build the booking page and reception screen first, run it next to your current system for two weeks, and only switch fully once reception prefers it. For salon groups and teams If you run more than one branch, or you have a manager, a marketing person and reception all touching the app, the Business plan adds a shared team workspace. Each person signs in with their own account and role (Admin, Editor, Viewer), you can keep internal apps members-only so only your staff can open them, and Google Workspace sign-in works if your salon uses Google for email. That's useful when the same workspace also holds a staff rota app or a stock list for each branch. Try it with your own services The fastest way to know if this route fits your salon is to paste your real service list into the first prompt and see what comes back. There's a salon booking system page with example prompts , and Mythex works fully in Arabic, so you can write the prompts in Arabic too. The Free plan is enough to build and test a first version; the plans and current prices are on the pricing page . Whatever you choose, write down your booking flow first. A salon that knows exactly how its bookings move will pick the right tool, whether it buys one or builds one.
